latin: Eucliō<sup>2</sup>, senex avārissimus, quī aurum suum in aululā quādam abscondit; sēcum loquitur. — Voluī* animum tandem cōnfirmāre hodiē meum, ut bene habērem mē fīliae nūptiīs<sup>3</sup>.
Veniō ad macellum, rogitō piscēs: indicant cārōs, agnīnam cāram, cāram būbulam, vitulīnam, cētum, porcīnam<sup>4</sup>, cāra omnia.
Atque eō fuērunt cāriōra quod<sup>5</sup> aes<sup>6</sup> nōn erat.
Abeō* īrātus illinc, quoniam nihil est quod emere possim.
Accessit animus ad meam sententiam, quam minimō<sup>7</sup> sūmptū fīliam ut nūptum<sup>8</sup> darem.
Nunc tusculum<sup>9</sup> ēmī hoc et corōnās flōreās<sup>10</sup>,
Haec impōnentur in focō nostrō Lārī<sup>11</sup>,
ut fortūnātās faciat nātae<sup>12</sup> nūptiās.
Sed quid ego cōnspicor<sup>13</sup>? Apertās aedēs nostrās! — Vōx in aedibus audītur.
Et strepitūst intus<sup>14</sup>. Num ego compīlor<sup>15</sup> miser?
Congriō, coquus, ad cēnam parandam missus, jam prīdem in Euclīonis culīna satagit<sup>16</sup>. — Aulam majōrem sī potes ē vīcīniā pete: haec parva est; capere nōn quit*<sup>17</sup>.

Eucliō. — Ēī mihi. Periī Hercle! Aurum rapitur, aula quaeritur. Apollō, quaesō subvenī mihi atque adjuvā! Cōnfīge<sup>18</sup> sagittīs<sup>19</sup> fūrēs<sup>20</sup> thēsaurāriōs<sup>21</sup>! — Domum irruit; clāmōrēs verberaque audiuntur.
latinAccented: Eúcliō<sup>2</sup>, senex avāríssimus, quī aurum suum in áululā quādam abscóndit; sēcum lóquitur. — Vóluī* ánimum tandem cōnfirmā́re hódiē meum, ut bene habḗrem mē fī́liae nū́ptiīs<sup>3</sup>.
Véniō ad macéllum, rógitō piscēs: índicant cārōs, agnī́nam cāram, cāram bū́bulam, vitulī́nam, cētum, porcī́nam<sup>4</sup>, cāra ómnia.
Atque eō fuḗrunt cāriṓra quod<sup>5</sup> aes<sup>6</sup> nōn erat.
Ábeō* īrā́tus illinc, quóniam nihil est quod émere possim.
Accéssit ánimus ad meam senténtiam, quam mínimō<sup>7</sup> sūmptū fī́liam ut nūptum<sup>8</sup> darem.
Nunc túsculum<sup>9</sup> ēmī hoc et corṓnās flṓreās<sup>10</sup>,
Haec impōnéntur in focō nostrō Lārī<sup>11</sup>,
ut fortūnā́tās fáciat nātae<sup>12</sup> nū́ptiās.
Sed quid ego cṓnspicor<sup>13</sup>? Apértās aedēs nostrās! — Vōx in áedibus audī́tur.
Et strepítūst intus<sup>14</sup>. Num ego compī́lor<sup>15</sup> miser?
Cóngriō, coquus, ad cēnam parándam missus, jam prīdem in Euclī́onis culī́na sátagit<sup>16</sup>. — Aulam majṓrem sī potes ē vīcī́niā pete: haec parva est; cápere nōn quit*<sup>17</sup>.

Eúcliō. — Ēī mihi. Périī Hercle! Aurum rápitur, aula quáeritur. Apóllō, quaesō súbvenī mihi atque ádjuvā! Cōnfī́ge<sup>18</sup> sagíttīs<sup>19</sup> fūrēs<sup>20</sup> thēsaurā́riōs<sup>21</sup>! — Domum írruit; clāmṓrēs verberáque audiúntur.
english: Euclio, a very miserly old man, who has hidden his gold in a little pot; he speaks [alone] (with himself). — At last I have [taken my courage in both hands] (wanted to fortify my mind) today, in order to [treat myself well] (subj. impft) for my daughter's wedding.
I go to the market, I [bargain over] (ask several times) the fish: [they are said to be] (they indicate) dear, the lamb dear, dear the beef, the veal, the tuna, the pork (see note 4).
[It was] (were) all the dearer [because I had] (was) no money.
I go away from there in anger, because there is nothing that I can buy.
[It came into my head] to marry my daughter at the [best price] (that I might marry I give).
Now I have just bought this pinch of incense and [these] crowns of flowers;
[they will be placed] (these will be placed) on the hearth for our [god] Lar,
so that he may make happy the wedding of my daughter.
But what do I see? [Our] house open! — A voice is heard in the house.
And [there is] a racket in there. Am I being robbed, wretch that I am?

Congrio, the cook who has been sent to prepare the meal, has been bustling for a long time in Euclio's kitchen. — Go and ask for a bigger pot if you can [from the neighbours] (in the neighbourhood): this one is small, [it does not hold enough] (to take it cannot).

Euclio. — Woe is me! I'm done for, by Hercules! My gold is being carried off; they're looking for the pot. Apollo, I beg you, help me! Pierce with your arrows these thieves of treasure! — He rushes into the house; cries and the sound of blows are heard.

footnotes: Contundo, -is, -ere, -tudi, -tusum, to crush, to bruise, to «manhandle» (with a bludgeoning instrument) = cum + tundo (pft: tutudi), to strike. Not to be confused with tondeo, -es, -ere, totondi, tonsum, to shear. The literal translation of the title would be: they have manhandled me badly.
Euclio, proper noun, gen. Euclionis, gives Euclion in French. Likewise below we will find Congrio, Congrion.
Nuptiae, -arum, f. pl., the wedding.
Bubulam, vitulinam, porcinam, understood carnem (cf. L. 58, N. 3). Cetus, -i, m., or cete, -is, n., big sea fish (cetacean); here very probably tuna, a relatively cheap fish.
Eo... quod, above all... because; and here, with the comparative (cariora), all the more... because.
Aes, aeris, n., bronze, money (coinage). Aes alienum, other people's money, debts.
Quam + superlative, the most... possible. Sumptus, -us, m., expense (sumere).
Nuptum, supine of nubere (cf. L. 43, N. 16).
Tus, turis, n., incense, perfume that was burnt in honour of the gods; whence its diminutive tusculum, not to be confused with the town of Tusculum, which we will find again L. 87, N. 12.
Floreus, -a, -um, adj., meaning made with flowers (flos, floris, m.).
Lar, Laris, m., the god Lar, protector of the family.
Natus, -i, son; noun formed from the past participle of nascor. Likewise nata, -ae, daughter (also written gnatus, gnata).
Conspicari, v. dep. t., to perceive.
Strepitust = strepitus est; abridged form that one meets often in Plautus. Strepitus, -us, m., noise, racket. Intus, adv., inside (cf. L. 80, N. 7).
Compilare, to pillage, to rob; here in the PASSIVE.
Satagere = satis agere (no supine), to have a lot to do.

Queo*, -is, -ire, quivi, quitum, to be capable of (+ inf.). Its opposite nequeo is much more used. Aula, -ae, f., the pot, whose diminutive aulula has given the title of the play, is an archaism. One now writes olla.
Configere, to pierce; we have seen figere (L. 44, N. 16).
Sagitta, -ae, f., arrow.
Fur, furis, m., thief. Trium litterarum homo (expression used by Plautus in the same play), man of (whose name is written in) three letters (F.U.R.).
Thesaurarius, -a, -um, adj., formed from thesaurus, -i, m., the treasure.
comments: N.B. — The play by Plautus is in verse, but as we have had to make modifications and cuts to it, we have not judged it proper to separate the lines from one another. You can therefore provisionally consider these extracts as prose.
Histrio, -onis, m., actor. — Acquiro, -is, -ere, quisivi, quisitum, to add to, to acquire. — Furnus, -i, m., oven. — Dissimilis is constructed with the DATIVE.

latin: Quandō vīvēbat Plautus?
Titus Maccius Plautus nātus annō 500° Ā.Ū.C. (ab Urbe conditā), ī.ē. annō 254 Ā.C. (ante Chrīstum nātum) et annō 184 Ā.C. mortuus esse crēditur.
Quamdiū vīxit? Sī haec tempora sine errōre cōnstant 70 annōs vīxit.
Quālīs fuit ejus vīta?
Dē eā nōn multa sānē nōvimus.
Juvenis histriō fuisse dīcitur, ē quōdam cōmoedōrum grege.
Deinde cōmoediās ipse scrīpsit, in quibus graecōs auctōrēs imitātus est.
Quam pecūniam theātrō acquīsīvit, eam negōtiandō perdidit.
Quārē tālī difficultāte nummāria labōrāvit ut apud pistōrem vīctum quaerere dēbuerit.
Dīcunt eum ante furnum, quotiēscumque ōtium adesset, cōmoediās etiam scrīpsisse.
Vīta et opera ejus haud dissimilia sunt vītae et operibus Johannis-Baptistae Poquelin, quī apud Gallōs Molière vocātur.
Exemplī grātia, auctor ille Gallus in eā cōmoediā, quae Avārus īnscrībitur, Plautī Aululāriam imitātus est.
latinAccented: Quandō vīvḗbat Plautus?
Titus Máccius Plautus nātus annō 500° Ā.Ū.C. (ab Urbe cónditā), ī.ē. annō 254 Ā.C. (ante Chrīstum nātum) et annō 184 Ā.C. mórtuus esse crḗditur.
Quámdiū vīxit? Sī haec témpora sine errṓre cōnstant 70 annōs vīxit.
Quālīs fuit ejus vīta?
Dē eā nōn multa sānē nṓvimus.
Júvenis hístriō fuísse dī́citur, ē quōdam cōmoedṓrum grege.
Deínde cōmóediās ipse scrīpsit, in quibus graecōs auctṓrēs imitā́tus est.
Quam pecū́niam theā́trō acquīsī́vit, eam negōtiándō pérdidit.
Quārē tālī difficultā́te nummā́ria labōrā́vit ut apud pistṓrem vīctum quáerere dēbúerit.
Dīcunt eum ante furnum, quotiēscúmque ṓtium adésset, cōmóediās étiam scrīpsísse.
Vīta et ópera ejus haud dissimília sunt vītae et opéribus Johánnis-Baptístae Póquelin, quī apud Gallōs Molíère vocā́tur.
Exémplī grā́tia, auctor ille Gallus in eā cōmóediā, quae Avā́rus īnscrī́bitur, Plautī Aululā́riam imitā́tus est.
english: When did Plautus live?

T. M. P. [is believed to have been] born in the year 500 [of the foundation of Rome] (since the city built), that is to say in 254 B.C. (before Christ born) and [to have died] in 184 B.C. (dead to be believed).
How long did he live? — If these [dates] (times) [are exact] (without error consistent), he lived 70 years.
What was his life like?
Of it we truly don't know much.
Young, it is said that he was an actor, [in] a troupe of comedians.
Then he himself wrote comedies, in which he imitated the Greek authors.
The money he earned thanks to the theatre, he lost it by going into business.
For this reason, he suffered such financial difficulties that he had to earn his living with a baker.
It is said that (him) in front of the oven, each time [he had leisure] (leisure was present), [he wrote] some more comedies (to have written).
His life and works [hardly differ] (are hardly different) from the life and works of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, who among the French is called Molière.
For example, this French author, in the comedy called The Miser, imitated the Aulularia of Plautus.

sources.english: (From the Aulularia (the [play] relating to the little pot) of Plautus (lines 371...395).)
